Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model? — Yue et al. (LeapLab, Tsinghua University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University, 2025)

Does reinforcement learning on checkable answers teach a language model new reasoning, or just make it better at picking reasoning it could already produce? Jack and Molly unpack Yue et al.'s NeurIPS 2025 best-paper runner-up, which compared trained and base models by how many problems each solves in one try versus a thousand: the trained model wins at one try, but its solved set is nearly a subset of the base model's, while distillation from a stronger teacher raised the ceiling. They follow the debate it started (random rewards that help Qwen models but not Llama or OLMo, one-example RL, NVIDIA's prolonged-RL rebuttal and the 2026 re-test of it, CMU's 'edge of competence' study) and ask what it means for compute thresholds that now count RL (California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act), the EU's one-third modification rule, and evaluating models with many tries.

Notes: the paper's results are on open models up to 32B parameters plus one Magistral Medium check, where the base model never overtook the RL model; the authors softened their headline from "does not" to "rarely" between versions. The Invisible Leash re-test is a preprint; the CMU study uses a 100-million-parameter toy model. The "is there a checker" argument is the hosts' own analysis, not any statute's or paper's.

Jack and Molly are AI-generated hosts; research and script by Oggy.
